Explanation—'Tattvavit yukta' - these words here are the speakers of the discerning practitioner of Yoga, who is eager to experience the ultimate reality like a great person, and has no relation (of doership) with the actions of Sānkhya. 
In him, such discernment has awakened that all actions are happening in nature, and I have no relation with those actions. 
He who never sees even a little bit of doership in himself, i.e., in his nature, is 'tattvavit'. 
In him, there is always a natural caution that there is no doership in the nature. 
He never accepts his oneness with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and life force, which are the actions of nature, so how can he consider the actions done by them as his own actions? 
Actually, the above state is of all human beings; 
but they mistakenly consider the nature as the doer of actions (Gita - twenty-seventh verse of the third chapter). 
The actions of the individual body are also happening by the same power of the Supreme Lord by which the actions of the entire world are happening. 
However, due to considering one's relation with the tiny part of the universe, a person starts considering some actions of the individual as his own actions. 
To remove this notion, the Lord says that the practitioner should never consider himself as the doer. 
As long as there is a notion of doership in any part, he is called a practitioner. 
When there is a complete absence of the notion of doership in oneself and one experiences one's nature, then he is called a tattvavit mahāpurusha. 
Just as a person has no relation with the dream after waking up, similarly, a tattvavit mahāpurusha has no relation with the actions happening through the body, etc. 
Here, 'tattvavit' is one who knows that all actions and qualities are in nature, and there are no qualities and actions in the ultimate reality beyond nature. 
The ultimate reality beyond nature is the illuminator and support of all, yet it is intertwined with the illuminated (the body, etc.). 
Although it is intertwined with the illuminated, the illuminator remains the illuminator, and the illuminated remains the illuminated. 
Similarly, it is the support of all, yet it is all-pervading in every particle of the supported; 
but it is never the supported, because there is no action or change in the illuminator and the support. 
Action and change are only in the illuminated or the supported. 
One who knows the distinction between the illuminator and the illuminated, the support and the supported, is 'tattvavit'. 
The Lord has also stated this knowledge of the distinction between nature (the field) and the knower of the field (the seventh chapter, fourth, fifth, and thirteenth verses, and the thirteenth chapter, second, nineteenth, twenty-third, and thirty-fourth verses). 

'Pashyan shrinvan sprishan' - here, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, and eating are the five actions of the five senses of knowledge (respectively, eyes, ears, skin, nose, and tongue). 
Walking, grasping, speaking, and excreting - these four actions are of the five organs of action (respectively, feet, hands, speech, genitals, and anus). 
Sleeping - this is one action of the internal organ. 
Breathing - this is one action of the life force, and opening the eyes * . 
Here, the actions of the five organs of action have been described under four actions, i.e., the actions of the genitals and anus have been described under the action of 'excreting'.
